dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, task-level deployment by identifying standardised, repeatable and outsourced transactional legal workflows as especially automatable. However, it departs materially from the cluster’s near-term human-led copilot and verification emphasis by arguing that buyers can trust AI output without deep legal expertise and by framing Harvey and other providers as moving toward autopilot.
qs: The work product is standardised enough that quality is verifiable, so the buyer can trust AI output without deep legal expertise.
Harvey is the emerging leader and is moving quickly to autopilot; Crosby and Lawhive are the autopilot-native newcomers.

kp.k: Selling work changes AI competition and revenue opportunities
kp.d: Bek predicts that the next $1T company will sell services delivered through software rather than software tools. He argues that model improvements threaten tool vendors with commoditisation but improve the speed, cost and competitiveness of providers selling completed work. His illustrative comparison is $10K annually for QuickBooks versus $120K for an accountant to close the books, not a reported study.
qs: The next $1T company will be a software company masquerading as a services firm.
If you sell the tool, you’re in a race against the model. But if you sell the work, every improvement in the model makes your service faster, cheaper, and harder to compete with.
A company might spend $10K a year for QuickBooks and $120K on an accountant to close the books.

kp.k: Intelligence and judgement distinguish automation opportunities
kp.d: Bek distinguishes complex but rule-governed execution, termed intelligence, from judgement requiring experience, taste and instinct. He asserts that AI can now perform most software-engineering intelligence work autonomously while humans retain judgement, and predicts this transition across professions. Supporting usage claims—that agents now start more tasks than humans and software engineering exceeds half of professional AI-tool usage—are presented without study details.
qs: Writing code is mostly *intelligence*. Knowing what to build next is *judgement*.
Software engineering accounts for over half of all AI tool usage across professions. Every other category is still in single digits.
AI has crossed the threshold where it can do most of the intelligence work autonomously and leave the judgement to humans.
Software engineering got there first. It is coming to every single profession.

kp.k: Autopilots sell outcomes directly rather than augmenting professionals
kp.d: Bek contrasts copilots such as Harvey selling tools to law firms, whose professionals retain responsibility for output, with autopilots such as Crosby selling NDA drafting directly to companies. He argues that sufficient model intelligence now supports starting with an autopilot in some categories, capturing work budgets rather than smaller tool budgets. The predicted speed of adoption depends on the proportion of intelligence work.
qs: A copilot sells the tool. An autopilot sells the work.
Harvey sells to law firms. Rogo sells to investment banks. The professional is the customer, the tool makes them more productive, and they take responsibility for the output.
Crosby sells to the company that needs an NDA drafted, not to outside counsel.
The higher the intelligence ratio in any field, the sooner autopilots will win.

kp.k: Proprietary data could expand automation into judgement
kp.d: Bek predicts that accumulated proprietary domain data about good judgement will shift the boundary of automatable work, eventually bringing copilots and autopilots together. He asserts that this transition has already begun in several categories, while stressing that initial market positioning determines which providers can acquire customers and build the data needed for broader capabilities.
qs: Today’s judgement will become tomorrow’s intelligence.
As AI systems accumulate proprietary data about what good judgement looks like in their domain, the frontier will shift.
Copilots and autopilots will converge.
But the starting position matters because it determines where autopilots can win customers now and begin compounding the data that will eventually let them handle judgement too.

kp.k: Existing outsourcing provides the recommended market-entry strategy
kp.d: Bek states that services spending is six times software spending and defines the eventual autopilot market as all insourced and outsourced labour spending in a category. He recommends entering through outsourced, intelligence-heavy tasks because buyers already accept external delivery, allocate budgets and purchase outcomes; subsequent expansion would target insourced, judgement-heavy work as AI capabilities compound.
qs: For every dollar spent on software, six are spent on services.
The total addressable market for autopilots is all labour spend in a category, insourced and outsourced combined.
Replacing an outsourcing contract with an AI-native services provider is a vendor swap. Replacing headcount is a reorg.
The playbook: companies should start with the outsourced, intelligence-heavy task. Nail distribution. Expand toward the insourced, judgement-heavy work as the AI compounds.

kp.k: Transactional legal work is positioned for direct substitution
kp.d: The illustrative opportunity map assigns transactional legal work a $20-25B labour market and characterises contract drafting, NDAs and regulatory filings as intelligence-heavy and routinely outsourced. Bek asserts that standardised outputs allow buyers without deep legal expertise to verify quality and trust AI output. He describes Harvey as moving toward autopilot and Crosby and Lawhive as autopilot-native entrants; Crosby's NDA focus illustrates his recommended entry strategy. These are the author's market and capability assessments, not findings from a presented legal-quality study.
qs: **Legal, transactional work ($20-25B). **Contract drafting, NDAs, regulatory filings: high intelligence, routinely outsourced.
The work product is standardised enough that quality is verifiable, so the buyer can trust AI output without deep legal expertise.
Harvey is the emerging leader and is moving quickly to autopilot; Crosby and Lawhive are the autopilot-native newcomers.
Crosby started with NDAs: a well-defined task, primarily intelligence, that most companies already outsource to external counsel.

kp.k: Copilot vendors face conflict with their professional customers
kp.d: Bek states that the fastest-growing AI companies in 2025 were copilots and predicts that many will attempt to become autopilots in 2026. Although they possess products and customer knowledge, he argues that selling completed work displaces their own customers' activities, creating an innovator's dilemma and an opening for providers built around direct outcome delivery.
qs: In 2025, the fastest-growing AI companies were copilots. In 2026, many will try to become autopilots.
They have the product and the customer knowledge.
But they also face the innovator’s dilemma: selling the work means cutting their own customers out of doing it.
That’s the opening for pure-play autopilots.

kp.k: Accounting shortages and tax complexity support automation
kp.d: Bek estimates US outsourced accounting and audit at $50-80B, stating that the US lost roughly 340,000 accountants over five years and that 75% of CPAs are nearing retirement. He argues that shortages, lengthy licensing and comparatively low starting salaries accelerate AI acceptance. For tax advisory, estimated at $30-35B, he calls CPA licensing a regulatory moat but describes 80-90% of work as intelligence; covering additional jurisdictions is predicted to strengthen providers' proprietary-data advantage. No underlying studies are supplied.
qs: **Accounting and audit ($50-80B outsourced in the US alone). **The US has lost roughly 340,000 accountants over five years while demand has grown.
75% of CPAs are nearing retirement, the licensing path is long, and starting salaries lag tech and finance.
That structural shortage is pushing firms to accept AI faster than almost any other profession.
**Tax advisory ($30-35B).** CPA licensing creates a regulatory moat, but 80-90% of the underlying work is intelligence.
Every additional jurisdiction a tax autopilot handles deepens its data moat.

kp.k: Insurance offers separate brokerage and claims automation opportunities
kp.d: Bek's illustrative map values insurance brokerage at $140-200B and claims adjusting at $50-80B including TPAs. He argues that standard commercial brokerage involves standardised carrier shopping and forms, while fragmented distribution prevents any single incumbent controlling customer relationships. Standard-line claims offer another opportunity because policy interpretation, damage schedules and actuarial tables structure the work, outsourcing is extensive and the workforce is aging. These are cross-domain mechanisms supporting his services thesis.
qs: **Insurance brokerage ($140-200B). **The largest dollar market on this list.
The distribution layer is incredibly fragmented, tens of thousands of small brokers each running the same process, so no single incumbent controls the customer relationship.
**Claims adjusting ($50-80B including TPAs). **On the other side of the insurance policy, claims adjusting is a separate autopilot surface.
Standard-line claims are settled by interpreting policy language against damage schedules and setting reserves using actuarial tables.
The market is massively outsourced to independents and TPAs like Crawford and Sedgwick.

kp.k: Healthcare billing illustrates rule-bound work within judgement-heavy professions
kp.d: Bek estimates outsourced US healthcare revenue-cycle work at $50-80B and distinguishes billing from the judgement commonly associated with healthcare. He characterises medical coding into approximately 70,000 standardised ICD-10 codes as complex but rule-governed, arguing that mature outcome-based outsourcing makes lower-cost substitution the principal autopilot proposition.
qs: **Healthcare revenue cycle ($50-80B outsourced in US)**.
People hear “healthcare” and assume it’s judgement-heavy, but the billing layer is almost pure intelligence.
Medical coding is translating clinical notes into ~70,000 standardised ICD-10 codes.
The outsourcing is already mature and outcome-based. An autopilot just has to do the same thing at lower cost.

kp.k: Managed IT presents repetitive outsourced tasks for outcome delivery
kp.d: Bek assigns IT managed services a $100B+ labour market and identifies patching, monitoring, user provisioning and alert triage as repetitive intelligence tasks. He contrasts software sold to managed service providers with the proposed direct sale of functioning IT to companies as an outcome, asserting that the latter offering has not yet been established.
qs: **IT managed services ($100B+).** Every SMB outsources its IT.
Patching, monitoring, user provisioning, alert triage: intelligence work running on repeat across thousands of identical environments.
The existing software layer (ConnectWise, Datto) sells tools to the MSP.
Nobody has yet sold “your IT runs” directly to the company as an outcome.

kp.k: Procurement automation can target previously uneconomic work
kp.d: For supply chain and procurement, estimated at $200B+, Bek proposes a different entry strategy: work currently neglected rather than already outsourced. He states that most enterprises negotiate seriously only with their top 20% of suppliers and that contract leakage represents 2-5% of total procurement spend. AI could pursue the remaining work without displacing an incumbent or substituting an existing budget.
qs: **Supply chain and procurement ($200B+).** Most enterprises negotiate seriously with only their top 20% of suppliers.
The long tail gets zero attention because it’s not economical to have humans do the work.
Contract leakage runs 2-5% of total procurement spend.
The wedge is abandoned work: no budget line to justify, no incumbent to displace, just found money.

kp.k: Recruitment and consulting show limits and task-level disaggregation
kp.d: Bek estimates recruitment and staffing at $200B+ and recommends high-volume, standardised matching as the autopilot entry point, distinguishing screening, matching and outreach from judgement-intensive candidate closing and culture-fit assessment. He estimates management consulting at $300-400B but calls it mostly judgement work, framing automation of data gathering and benchmarking while humans retain strategic recommendations as an open question rather than an established transition.
qs: The top of the hiring funnel (screening, matching, outreach) is pure intelligence, but closing a candidate and assessing culture fit is judgement built on years of pattern recognition.
The autopilot wedge exists in high-volume, low-judgement roles where matching is standardised.
**Management consulting ($300-400B). **Huge market but the work is mostly judgement.

The interesting question is whether AI can disaggregate consulting into intelligence components (data gathering, benchmarking) and judgement components (strategic recommendations), with the intelligence layer getting automated and the judgement layer staying human.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Bek predicts that AI-native companies selling completed work rather than software tools will capture service budgets and benefit directly from improving models.
pts.d: Across professional services, Julien Bek argues that tool vendors risk having their products absorbed into foundation-model capabilities, whereas outcome-selling providers become faster and cheaper as models improve. He predicts a trillion-dollar company built on this model and defines its long-term addressable market as both outsourced and internally performed labour. His copilot/autopilot distinction concerns selling tools to professionals versus selling work directly to buyers; it does not establish that every such provider operates without human involvement.

pts.k: Bek identifies standardised transactional legal work as an immediate market for AI-native outcome providers.
pts.d: Bek places contract drafting, NDAs and regulatory filings in a $20–25 billion labour market that he describes as rules-based and routinely outsourced. He claims that standardisation makes quality verifiable enough for buyers without deep legal expertise to trust AI output. He presents Harvey as a tool provider to law firms that is moving toward autopilot, and Crosby and Lawhive as autopilot-native newcomers. Crosby's direct sale of NDA drafting to companies illustrates substitution for work otherwise purchased from outside counsel.

pts.k: Bek predicts that automation will spread from rules-based work to judgement, with outsourced tasks providing the initial entry point.
pts.d: Bek distinguishes 'intelligence'—executing complex but rule-governed tasks—from judgement grounded in experience and taste. He argues that software engineering has already crossed a threshold for autonomous intelligence work and predicts the same progression across professions. He expects proprietary domain data to make judgement increasingly automatable, bringing copilots and autopilots together. His recommended strategy is to replace outsourced tasks first, then expand into internal and judgement-heavy work.

pts.k: Bek maps different automation opportunities across services according to task structure, outsourcing and labour-market conditions.
pts.d: Beyond law, Bek identifies standard commercial insurance brokerage, healthcare billing, standard-line claims adjusting, tax work and recurring IT operations as promising rules-based service markets. He argues that accountant shortages accelerate AI acceptance; procurement offers an opportunity to perform previously uneconomic work rather than displace incumbents; recruitment offers an initial opening in standardised high-volume matching; and consulting may be split into automated intelligence work and human strategic judgement. These are differentiated opportunity claims, not a prediction of simultaneous replacement across all services.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Bek supports the thesis with market-size and workforce figures, adoption assertions, named companies and business-model reasoning; the document supplies no cited studies or legal-output performance tests.
pts.d: The numerical basis includes a six-to-one services/software spending ratio, a $20–25 billion transactional legal market estimate, software engineering's reported share of AI-tool usage, and accountant workforce figures. Bek uses Harvey, Crosby, Lawhive and other named companies as illustrations of provider strategies. Crosby's NDA offering supports his outsourcing-entry argument, but the document gives no measured cost savings, legal accuracy results, customer outcomes or method for verifying legal quality. The trillion-dollar prediction, eventual automation of judgement and claims about frictionless substitution are presented as strategic arguments rather than demonstrated findings. The quantitative assertions are not accompanied by sources or methodologies in the supplied text.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Writing on March 5, 2026, Bek presents direct outcome-selling as viable now in selected categories and predicts a broader copilot-to-autopilot shift during 2026.
pts.d: Bek contrasts copilot growth in 2025 with expected transition attempts in 2026. He says the transition has already begun in several categories, but conditions early success on a high proportion of rules-based work, existing outsourcing, clear scope, an established budget and effective distribution. Expansion into judgement depends on accumulating proprietary domain data. He provides no deadline for universal professional adoption, full convergence, capture of internal labour budgets or the emergence of a trillion-dollar company. The opportunity map is expressly illustrative, and consulting automation is framed as an open question.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted shift changes who buys AI and who performs the work: professional tool users may become displaced intermediaries, while business clients buy outcomes directly.
pts.d: In law, Bek contrasts law firms buying Harvey to improve professional productivity with companies buying NDA drafting directly from Crosby. Under the copilot model, professionals retain responsibility for output; under his autopilot model, the client purchases the outcome rather than a tool for outside counsel. Existing outsourced providers face replacement first, while internal employees enter the longer-term expansion opportunity. Copilot vendors face conflict with their professional customers if they start selling competing services, creating an opening for AI-native service providers. Across other sectors, affected buyers include CFOs, SMBs and enterprise procurement teams; affected providers include accountants, brokers, adjusters, IT service providers, recruiters and consultants. The legal discussion concerns transactional business services, not an explicit claim about unmet civil legal need or access to justice.
